title: Quantifying Ion‐Specific Effects on the Size‐Exclusion Transport of Multi‐Sized Colloids in Porous Media Using a Novel Synthetic DNA Labeling Approach
content:
Abstract

Colloids strongly adsorb pollutants and promote their co-transport in aquatic environments, posing substantial ecological contamination risks. However, quantifying the size exclusion effect (SEE), a critical mechanism that enhances colloid transport, remains challenging in multi-sized colloid systems, owing to limited high-resolution labeling methods and ion-induced dynamic aggregation. Here, we developed a high-resolution DNA-based tracing framework that employs synthetic DNA fragments to individually label multi-sized colloids (0.1, 0.2, 0.5, and 1.0 μm), and utilizes quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) to quantify their transport behavior in saturated quartz sand under the typical environmental ions (NaCl/CaCl2). The results demonstrated that Ca2+ promoted colloid aggregation and retention more strongly than Na+, thereby modifying size-exclusion behavior, although the magnitude of SEE depended on colloid size and transport conditions. While the SEE generally exhibited a positive size dependence in the single-sized system, the multi-sized system exhibited higher SEE for 0.1 and 0.2 μm colloids relative to their single-sized counterparts under certain solution chemistry conditions. This discrepancy may be attributed to pore blockage caused by larger colloids within the multi-sized system. Furthermore, two transport patterns, blocking and ripening, were identified from the breakthrough curves of DNA-labeled colloids. Correlation analysis revealed that the SEE parameter (γ) was positively correlated with the normalized retention parameter (S max/C 0) under blocking conditions (r = 0.655). This study highlights the effectiveness of synthetic DNA labeling approach in tracking the transport of multi-sized colloids, providing new insights into the fate of colloids in natural and engineered porous systems.
